clue.text: Until you run out of rope, far from a sweet beginning.

definitions.text: Until you run out of rope
definitions.meaning: first meaning: on a ship the bitter end is the last part of a rope or cable, so this phrase means right to the very last

definitions.text: far from a sweet beginning
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: a bitter finish is the opposite of a sweet start

explanation.walkthrough: The bitter end is a sailor's term for the inboard end of an anchor cable, which is where the everyday idiom comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means persisting to the last possible point, however unpleasant, and its words also describe a sour conclusion.

clue.text: What the old singer was doing in the tulip garden shouldn't have created a lot of noise.

definitions.text: What the old singer was doing in the tulip garden shouldn't have created a lot of noise.

parts.words: What the old singer was doing in the tulip garden
parts.note: Tiny Tim's falsetto novelty hit of 1968 had him stepping softly among the tulips

parts.words: shouldn't have created a lot of noise
parts.note: moving on the points of one's feet is how one walks quietly

explanation.surface: A veteran crooner pottering among the flowerbeds ought to have kept the noise down.
explanation.walkthrough: The singer is Tiny Tim, whose falsetto 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips' made him famous; the second half confirms the answer is a quiet way of walking.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title action is stepping softly on the toes, a manner of walking that makes little sound.

clue.text: Asked for a bit of money? Little Edward has a word of pain internally.

definitions.text: Asked for a bit of money

indicators.note: internally tells us the cry of pain sits inside the short name for Edward

parts.note: Ted is a familiar short form of Edward
the cry someone gives when hurt

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a request for cash is behind young Edward's cries of pain.
explanation.definitionFit: To touch someone for money is an idiom meaning to ask them for a small loan or gift.

clue.text: The strange device on a poetic banner. (Just like a bit of straw!)

definitions.text: The strange device on a poetic banner
definitions.meaning: first meaning: in Longfellow's poem '...' a youth carries a banner 'with the strange device, ...!'

definitions.text: Just like a bit of straw!
definitions.meaning: second meaning: fine wood shavings used for packing, much like straw

explanation.walkthrough: The poem is Longfellow's, whose climber keeps crying the Latin motto; in America the same word names wood-wool packing material.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto meaning 'ever higher' is the poem's banner text, and is also the trade name for shredded-wood packing.

clue.text: Where they race you find your insides show it.

definitions.text: Where they race

indicators.note: the inner letters of the words find and your display the answer, so it is tucked within them

parts.note: the run of letters the answer is taken from

explanation.surface: At a racetrack, you sense your stomach betraying your nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your insides' looks like talk of nerves, but it points at the letters inside the words beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Indianapolis, home of the famous 500-mile motor race, is known for short by this nickname.

clue.text: He sits with his chin in his hands, being the skinny type when the frog is half there.

definitions.text: He sits with his chin in his hands

parts.note: taken as written
a thin person is the skinny sort

indicators.note: only half of the frog's name is present, the first three of its six letters

parts.note: Kermit is the famous Muppet frog

explanation.surface: Someone describes a slender person posing chin on hands while the frog is half absent.
explanation.walkthrough: The frog is Kermit of the Muppets; keep the front half of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodin's famous bronze sculpture shows a seated man resting his chin on his hand, deep in thought.

clue.text: It's OK to say this just before you quit talking, and "out with it!"

definitions.text: It's OK to say this just before you quit talking, and "out with it!"

parts.words: It's OK to say this just before you quit talking
parts.note: radio operators acknowledge a message with this word, meaning received and understood
the radio sign-off 'over and out' has a variant ending with the same word followed by 'and out'

explanation.surface: A radio etiquette tip: what it is fine to say at the end of a conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue builds the radio phrase in which the word is followed by 'out'; read together with the quoted bit it gives the full sign-off.
explanation.definitionFit: In radio procedure this word signals that a message has been received and understood, so it is a way of saying okay.

clue.text: Have to have come first, being so teased.

definitions.text: teased

parts.note: to need to do something is to have to do it
to have led is to have been in front

explanation.surface: Someone is ribbed for always insisting on being first.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or goad them with small jibes, a synonym for teasing.

clue.text: One of the original dogooders.

definitions.text: One of the original dogooders.

parts.note: points to the first, archetypal example, the man in Jesus's parable
people who help others, sometimes said mockingly; the answer's first word is buried in it

explanation.walkthrough: The parable in Luke's Gospel tells of a traveller from Samaria who helps a beaten stranger; the phrase now names any kindly helper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase from the parable is the archetype of a person who helps a stranger in need without reward.

clue.text: What the predator possibly did has little weight in the police department.

definitions.text: What the predator possibly did

indicators.note: in places the small unit of weight inside the abbreviation for the police department

parts.note: PD is the American abbreviation for police department
an ounce is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A detective theory: what the predator did involves something light at police headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: A predator springs suddenly on its prey, which is to leap or swoop on it.

clue.text: This artist's neighbors referred to him mainly by his origins.

definitions.text: This artist's neighbors referred to him mainly by his origins.

parts.words: This artist's neighbors referred to him
parts.note: the painter Domenikos Theotokopoulos lived in Toledo, where the Spanish knew him by a nickname
the nickname means 'the Greek', naming the land he came from, Crete

explanation.surface: An artist's neighbours mostly called him by where he came from.
explanation.walkthrough: The painter was born in Crete and worked in Spain, where his Greek surname proved too long, so locals called him by his nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname is Spanish for 'the Greek', the name by which the Cretan-born painter of Toledo is known.

clue.text: How we don't like to be on the phone.

definitions.text: How we don't like to be on the phone.

parts.words: How we don't like to be
parts.note: names an unwelcome state, which a solver first reads as a mood or manner
pins it to telephone calls, where callers are left waiting with music playing

explanation.surface: A grumble about the thing nobody enjoys when calling a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Being kept waiting on a telephone line, usually to recorded music, is the unpopular state the phrase describes.

clue.text: What the one in poetry did in his glee.

definitions.text: What the one in poetry did in his glee.

parts.words: What the one in poetry did
parts.note: the boy who slays the beast in Lewis Carroll's 'Jabberwocky' and is greeted by his father
the poem has the father laughing 'in his joy', a word Lewis Carroll invented for it

explanation.surface: Asking what a poem's hero did in his happiness.
explanation.walkthrough: Carroll coined the word in 'Jabberwocky', blending chuckle and snort; it has since entered the dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: The coined word means laughed in a breathy, gleeful way, which is what the father in the poem does.

clue.text: By itself, you get a ringer, but she had a helluva environment part of the time!

definitions.text: she had a helluva environment part of the time

parts.note: per se is Latin for 'by itself' or 'in itself'
a telephone is something that rings

explanation.surface: A remark that one thing alone makes a bell, and a woman who spent time somewhere hellish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A ringer' looks like a lookalike or a bell, but here it is simply the thing that rings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this goddess spends part of every year in the underworld as Hades' queen, a literal hell of a setting.

clue.text: Where we used to watch movies had quite a racket around almost all of the stream.

definitions.text: Where we used to watch movies

indicators.note: around puts the noise on both sides of the shortened stream

parts.note: a din is a loud noise

indicators.note: almost all of the word drops its final letter

parts.note: a river is a large stream

explanation.surface: Nostalgia for an old cinema whose surroundings were noisy and near water.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-air cinema where people watched films from their parked cars, popular in mid-century America.

clue.text: Teams display at least one point on a fateful day.

definitions.text: Teams

indicators.note: on means the point is placed next to the day, coming first

parts.note: S is one of the compass points
the Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was assassinated

explanation.surface: Sports teams show off at least one point scored on a big day.
explanation.definitionFit: Teams in a game are the opposing sides, a common synonym.

clue.text: Song of a May-December romance?

definitions.text: Song of a May-December romance?

parts.note: the Kurt Weill and Maxwell Anderson standard titled after the month followed by the word 'Song'
a romance between a young and an old partner; the song has an ageing man courting, and this month falls between May and December

explanation.walkthrough: The standard sung by an older suitor who reminds his love the days grow short when you reach this month.
explanation.definitionFit: In the famous song the month stands for late life, the older partner in a romance across ages.

clue.text: See 8
Poet who suggests he was not just a comer.

definitions.text: Poet

indicators.note: suggests means the poet's name only sounds like the word, not that it is spelt that way

parts.note: comings and goings: someone who goes as well as comes is a goer

explanation.surface: A poet's name hints that he did more than merely arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: John Gower was a medieval English poet and friend of Chaucer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gower wrote the 'Confessio Amantis' and is one of the major English poets of the fourteenth century.

clue.text: Like a certain coyote, at best!

definitions.text: Like a certain coyote, at best!

parts.note: the cartoon character Wile E. Coyote, whose name puns on wily
asks for the superlative form, the most of that quality

explanation.surface: A wry aside comparing someone to a famous cartoon coyote, at the most generous.
explanation.walkthrough: Wile E. Coyote chases the Road Runner in Warner Bros. cartoons; his name sounds like 'wily'.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of wily means most cunning, the trait the cartoon coyote's name claims for him.

clue.text: Not the usual phrases that describe those who carry certain loads.

definitions.text: those who carry certain loads

indicators.note: the letters are not in their usual order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark about unusual expressions used for people who bear heavy burdens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phrases' looks like the subject being discussed, but its letters are the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan people famed as mountain guides and porters carry expedition loads up to high camps.

clue.text: Being sent to it wasn't pleasant, the point being made to Spain and Portugal.

definitions.text: Being sent to it wasn't pleasant

parts.note: S, the compass point south
Iberia is the peninsula they share

explanation.surface: A grim exile, with a point being made to the Iberian nations.
explanation.definitionFit: Russian and Soviet rulers banished prisoners and dissidents to this remote and freezing region.

clue.text: The derring-do kind are shown in this sort of print, at times.

definitions.text: The derring-do kind
definitions.meaning: first meaning; plural here, while the answer reads as a singular phrase

definitions.text: this sort of print
definitions.meaning: second meaning: heavy, thick lettering used for emphasis

explanation.surface: Daring people appear in heavy lettering now and then, as in news headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Types' does double duty: kinds of people and printer's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy-weight printed letters are called this, and daring characters can be described as such types.

clue.text: A stage performance that's really bad should go off with a bang!

definitions.text: A stage performance that's really bad
definitions.meaning: first meaning: in American usage a show that flops is this

definitions.text: should go off with a bang
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an explosive device, the thing that ought to explode

explanation.surface: A dreadful show ought to end with a dramatic flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: In the US a flop is this; in Britain the same phrase 'went a bomb' oddly means a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a theatrical flop and an explosive device built to detonate.

clue.text: All together, boys!

definitions.text: All together, boys!

parts.note: the musical direction telling every player or singer to perform at once
the conductor seems to address the band, setting the instruction in the orchestra

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian term appears in scores where the whole ensemble joins in after a solo passage.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for 'all', the score marking calls on every performer in the ensemble to play at once.

clue.text: Proving a belonger has to show an arm or a leg.

definitions.text: a belonger
definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who belongs to a club or group

definitions.text: an arm or a leg
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a limb of the body

explanation.surface: Proof of club membership costs an arm and a leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An arm or a leg' echoes the idiom for a high price, but here it means a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both one who belongs to an organisation and a limb of the body.

clue.text: The bad mark given a nonunion type.

definitions.text: The bad mark
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the crust that forms over a wound

definitions.text: a nonunion type
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a worker who refuses to join a strike or union

explanation.surface: A disapproving record is given to someone who won't join the union.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the crust over a healing wound and also a strikebreaker, a worker scorned by union members.

clue.text: Miss West has the wrong sort of musical leader…

definitions.text: musical leader

parts.note: Mae West, the American actress

indicators.note: wrong means the letters of sort are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mae West is said to have the wrong kind of bandleader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong sort of' reads as a criticism, but 'sort' is the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A distinguished conductor or master musician is addressed by this Italian title for a master.

clue.text: …but at least this is a good musical.

definitions.text: …but at least this is a good musical.

parts.note: continues the previous clue, contrasting its wrong sort of thing with a right one
points at the Kander and Ebb hit set in a Berlin nightclub

explanation.surface: Following the complaint, a consolation: at least the show was a good one.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a sequel to the one before it, so read the pair together.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kander and Ebb show set in 1930s Berlin won the Tony for Best Musical and became a famous film.

clue.text: Evidently the finding of gold was a good deal, if you make a deal this way.

definitions.text: Evidently the finding of gold was a good deal, if you make a deal this way.

parts.words: Evidently the finding of gold was a good deal
parts.note: a lucky discovery of gold is a strike, and a good deal is a bargain

parts.words: if you make a deal this way
parts.note: the whole phrase is the idiom for agreeing terms

explanation.surface: A prospector's lucky find turned out to be good value, and the phrase for closing a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the answer says 'a strike is a bargain', which is what a gold strike is.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to agree terms with someone, to conclude a deal.
